Opinion Academia The middle-income health trap When a country crosses the World Bank’s threshold from low- to middle-income status, it is deemed too rich to qualify for aid, even though it is not yet rich enough to cover its health costs. Share this article Change text size Gift Premium Articles to Anyone I n the lexicon of development, few words sound as reassuring as “graduation,” which suggests progress past critical milestones and an escape from dependency. In global health, however, graduation increasingly creates a trap. When a country crosses the World Bank’s threshold from low- to middle-income status, it is deemed too rich to qualify for aid, even though it is not yet rich enough to cover its health costs. The implications of reaching this milestone (which is based on gross national income per capita) are therefore profound. Achieving middle-income status means that concessional loans will increasingly have to be replaced by market-rate borrowing, and that grants will shrink or disappear as global health programs wind down. But pathogens do not recognize income thresholds, and the resources available to health systems do not necessarily grow smoothly with GDP. In many countries, disease burdens remain stubbornly high long after aid eligibility has expired. If there is any lag in the growth of the government’s fiscal capacity, the result will be a widening gap between health needs and health financing. Neither markets nor donors are well equipped to fill it. This is a massive problem. Middle-income countries now account for over 70 percent of the world’s poor, for most deaths from tuberculosis, and for a still-high share of deaths from HIV and non-communicable diseases. Yet they receive a shrinking share of global health assistance, which is increasingly concentrated in a small number of fragile, low-income states. If graduation to middle-income status reliably coincided with robust tax systems, deep capital markets and comprehensive insurance schemes, it would make sense for recent grads to fend for themselves. But many middle-income countries face rising debt-service costs and collect less than 15 percent of GDP in taxes, owing to their large informal sectors. They may be richer on paper, but their health ministries are often poorer in practice. When donor-funded programs supported by institutions such as Gavi or the Global Fund taper off, governments are expected to assume full financial responsibility for vaccines, antiretrovirals and malaria control, often within the space of a few budget cycles. But such costs are often large, recurrent and have low visibility, which weakens political incentives to prioritize them over other spending. When the government failed to cover this new funding gap, harm-reduction services collapsed, and the country experienced a resurgence of infections among vulnerable populations. Composite: Guardian Design/AFP/Getty/Shutterstock/Rex Lyra McKee ‘Could only have been one person’: top former detective says system failed murdered journalist Lyra McKee Jason Murphy believes he knows who killed McKee in Derry, but culture of silence and mistrust of police is denying her family justice Michael Segalov Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.01 EDT Share When Lyra McKee was shot and killed on the night of 18 April 2019, approximately 150 people were in her vicinity. The 29-year-old journalist had watched in a crowd as rioting broke out in Derry, Northern Ireland . Police footage captured the grainy outline of a man firing a handgun. “Someone’s fucking shot,” a bystander could be heard crying in mobile phone footage shown as evidence in court. “There’s a fucking kid shot in the head.” The New IRA has claimed responsibility for her death. This July, more than seven years after McKee was killed, a Belfast judge delivered a verdict after a 25-month trial. Three men were found not guilty of her murder among a series of mostly failed prosecutions. The judgment criticised the prosecution’s case, in particular the lack of evidence identifying the defendants as those depicted, often masked, in video footage. None of the many onlookers on the street that night came forward as a witness to the murder. Jason Murphy was head of major investigations for the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) when McKee was killed. The former detective superintendent oversaw homicide investigations across Northern Ireland’s six counties while running his own caseload, including McKee’s murder. Next week Channel 4 will air a three-part documentary on his investigation. View image in fullscreen Jason Murphy was the lead investigator in the Lyra Mckee murder trial in Northern Ireland. Photograph: Polly Garnett/The Guardian Murphy is confident that he successfully identified the shooter, who he believes “could only have been one person”. But while the suspect was arrested, they were not charged. The prosecuting barrister felt that based on the evidence they could present in court, a guilty verdict was not likely. No eyewitness would confirm their identity. Within days of the killing, the New IRA offered its “full and sincere apologies” to McKee’s family, but no individual was held responsible. Murphy believes that a culture of silence within this tight-knit community – partly owing to a severe mistrust of the police, and partly out of fear of violent repercussions from allies of those implicated – is denying the McKee family justice for Lyra. “She was an innocent bystander,” he says. “Quickly it was clear this was an attack on the police.” It was a challenging investigation. McKee, who was from a Catholic background, was shot on the Creggan estate, one of Northern Ireland’s last IRA hotbeds. During the Troubles, the mostly Catholic area was a violent battleground, and it remains hostile territory for the PSNI. People here were reluctant to help “find someone within their own community who killed one of their own”, Murphy says. After McKee’s death, threatening graffiti appeared across Derry and placards were tied to lamp-posts warning of repercussions for providing information to the police. “Informers will be shot. IRA,” read one, illustrated with a rat in crosshairs. View image in fullscreen Lyra McKee rose to prominence in 2014 after a blog post titled ‘Letter to my 14-year-old self’, in which she spoke about growing up gay in Belfast. Photograph: Chiho Tang/Oranga Creative/PA Simple tasks were resource intensive, with two public order units enlisted to support each house search. The murder weapon wasn’t initially recovered from the scene, meaning “there were firearms circulating in the community, uncontrolled”. Acquiring bystander mobile phone footage required “court warrants to do searches and seize mobile phones from teenagers”. This was out of necessity, but also to ensure that children weren’t targeted in revenge, Murphy says. Early on in the investigation, he learned that the TV presenter Reggie Yates had been filming in Derry the night McKee was shot. A group of young men were showing Yates around the Creggan area for an MTV documentary about the impact of Brexit, though in her judgment, Mrs Justice Smyth stated it appeared Yates had been “making a documentary about Saoradh”, widely understood to be the political wing of the New IRA. In the footage, Yates is told by one man, Patrick Gallagher, that there “could be a number of people gathered” outside a property being searched by police, including “those that are more than capable of carrying out acts of resistance”. One of the last moments filmed is a woman pleading with Yates: “The rioting is going on because of the camera crew … it’s all set up for youse.” The cameras are switched off before McKee is shot. Days later the BBC interviewed Gallagher for a Newsnight segment . He was asked if he was surprised nobody had been charged with McKee’s murder. “Not really,” he replied. “People have called for members of this community to inform … but the people of this community know the life of an informer. Judging by history, they know exactly what would happen.” Originally from Belfast, McKee had moved to Derry to live with her partner. Her book Angels with Blue Faces, about a Troubles-era murder, was published soon after her death. She rose to prominence in 2014 after a blog post titled “Letter to my 14-year-old self”, in which she spoke about the struggle of growing up gay in Belfast. The letter was later turned into a short film. Three men found not guilty of murdering journalist Lyra McKee Read more While McKee was not the intended target of the New IRA, which said she was “tragically killed while standing beside enemy forces”, the prosecution’s case was still “that Lyra had been killed in a coordinated attack by members of the New IRA”, Murphy says. It also argued that “connectivity between mobile phones showed a direct relationship between the riot and known New IRA leadership. Therefore, the riot and shooting of Lyra were one continuous event.” In total, 10 men were charged with 52 offences . Gallagher was one of them. Three were charged with joint enterprise murder. None were alleged to have fired the gun, but to have intentionally encouraged or assisted the shooter. Separately, Niall Sheerin was sentenced to seven years in prison for possessing the murder weapon. Of the nine men ultimately prosecuted (the 10th died last year), seven were acquitted on all counts by the judge, including the three charged with murder and Gallagher. Kieran McCool was found guilty of common assault, and Christopher Gillen of possessing and throwing petrol bombs, and riot. Due to the risk of paramilitary interference, there was no jury. Murphy and his team “fully expected” to secure the “vast majority” of prosecutions, including the murder charges. The defence called no witnesses and presented a small amount of evidence. The prosecution faced further difficulty when some of the little identification evidence presented was dismissed by the court after police errors. A firewall was constructed between Murphy’s team and other PSNI officers tasked with identifying suspects. “Unbeknown to me, one of my team had visited the office of some of [these] officers,” says Murphy. “Those conversations should never have taken place.” Had that evidence been considered, Murphy concedes case outcomes “could have been” different against some defendants, though there were “multiple strands the judge didn’t agree with”. View image in fullscreen Lyra McKee’s sister Nichola Corner said she felt let down and that some people were ‘withholding evidence’. Photograph: PA He believes McKee’s family are likely to feel let down by the police and prosecution. “I felt ashamed to be part of a system that failed this family and community,” Murphy says. “I hoped the judgment would be the start of the grieving processes for Lyra’s family.” He says the case raises uncomfortable questions for the Northern Irish authorities. “How do we bring terrorist cases before the courts, with a realistic chance of conviction?” he asks. “If we can’t convict on the basis of five hours of documentary footage that has almost the totality of events, what else can we do?” He believes the outcome risks reinforcing “fears from the public: ‘Why put my head above the parapet, give evidence in court, to have them found not guilty?’” Nichola Corner, Lyra’s sister, says she feels “really, really let down”. She adds: “Some people have evidence that would assist us and are choosing to withhold it.” The Murder Detective starts on 26 August at 9pm on Channel 4 Explore more on these topics Lyra McKee Northern Ireland Crime Police Television Derry New IRA Share Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/21/more.text: The number of Russian citizens legally residing in the EU has grown by 105,000 since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, reaching 876,600 by the end of 2025, an analysis of Eurostat data shows.The figure represents a 13.6% rise from the 771,800 Russians holding valid temporary or permanent residence permits across EU member states in 2021. Germany hosts the largest community, with 218,000 residents, followed by Spain (116,800) and Estonia (78,400).Southern Europe has seen the sharpest growth: Spain issued residence permits to 44,400 Russian nationals over the period, France 13,700, while Cyprus and Portugal saw their Russian-born populations increase 2.5 and 3.5 times, respectively.Several EU states have moved in the opposite direction. Latvia, Estonia and the Czech Republic have recorded the largest drops in Russian residents, driven by tough migration policies and, in the Baltic states, security concerns over large Russian-speaking communities.Significant communities have also formed outside the EU. In Serbia the Russian population rose from roughly 5,000 before the invasion to 61,900 by the end of 2025. By spring of this year, Kazakhstan had absorbed more than 107,000 Russian migrants, while Armenia and Georgia hosted 43,500 and 70,000, respectively.Turkey drew large numbers in the immediate post-invasion period but later tightened residency rules. By June, valid Russian permits there had fallen to 75,900, half the 2023 peak.Researchers tracking emigration patterns have identified at least four distinct waves since February 2022. The most recent, running from this spring, has been sparked by renewed claims of impending mobilisation for Moscow's all-out war in Ukraine."Everyone now understands that they have no future in Russia. There is no image of the future, no understanding of what will happen in six months or a year," said Anastasia Burakova, a lawyer and founder of Kovcheg, a legal assistance project for Russians abroad. "What is more, there are risks linked to mobilisation and conscription, which people feel very personally."'Now I have nothing and I feel free'Ivan, 19, left Russia this spring to avoid conscription and now works in construction in Yerevan, posting videos on YouTube. A year earlier he had been a mobile phone store manager."I thought: this is it, this is life, everything is going the way it should," he said in a YouTube video. "Now I'm sitting on a bench in Yerevan, with no title and no steady job. My wife is next to me. Back then I was a manager and felt trapped. Now I have nothing, and I feel free."Surveys by independent researchers show the Russian emigrees include predominantly young couples, often without children, with both partners under 36.They tend to have high levels of education and are concentrated in professions either vulnerable to political repression — journalists, human rights workers, political analysts — or in high international demand, particularly IT, engineering and academia. Around 20% of those who left do not hold university degrees. Some 18% are studying or plan to study abroad.They fall into three broad groups: those who have settled and expect to remain abroad long-term, those who have already moved once and are preparing to relocate again, and those still in Russia who intend to leave within six months.The economic impact on host countries has been visible yet uneven. In Armenia and Georgia, the sudden influx of people and capital contributed to GDP growth of between 9% and 9.4% at its peak between 2022 and 2024, according to analysis published by the CASE Center research institute.Average Russian household incomes in Serbia ran to around €3,500 per month against a local average of €900. In Georgia the figures were €3,300 against €650. The effect has since moderated as host economies adapted, with growth settling back to 5–7% annually.Rather than competing for local jobs, most Russian migrants have worked remotely or set up their own businesses.In IT, up to 41% have maintained income from foreign clients, while in the media sector around 21% have done so, channelling money into host economies through taxes and everyday spending.Meanwhile, Russian authorities and independent researchers have documented some returns, but the scale remains disputed.The independent OutRush sociological project estimated that no more than 8% of emigrants had returned to Russia by summer 2024, with around 5% more intending to do so.The Institute of Applied Economic Research at RANEPA, a state-linked academic institution, put the overall return rate from the 2022–2023 wave at roughly 10%.Estimates from consulting firms and recruitment agencies are considerably higher, ranging from 16% among IT workers to 40–45% of those who left at the peak.Commonly cited reasons for returning include difficulty finding work, legal status problems and the closure of relocated Russian businesses.Russia's own official resettlement programme recorded a historic low in 2025, drawing only 26,700 people into the country.Euronews could not independently verify Russian government data.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/07/peac.text: During his sixth apostolic journey, Pope Leo XIV stopped in Paysandú, in Uruguay, where he celebrated Mass in the Parque París Londres in front of more than 40,000 faithful.Arriving at the exhibition area in the popemobile from the "Brigadier General Aviator Tydeo Larre Borges" International Airport, the Pontiff made his way through the cheering crowd, blessing those present. When he reached the altar, next to an image of Blessed Jacinto Vera, he centred his entire homily on the key concepts of unity and community."Peace is possible and we are called to build it," the pontiff said during the liturgical celebration. He then offered the multitude three symbols characteristic of Uruguayan soil to show how to safeguard and spread the Christian faith today.The first element he evoked was the "General Artigas" bridge, a metaphor for the importance of building strong bonds and engaging in dialogue with others. The second was represented by the local palm trees, which grow together in groves and recall the communal nature of the Church. Finally, there was mate, the famous traditional drink shared at moments of encounter, highlighted as a deep emblem of familiarity and brotherhood. "An element deeply significant to your culture, around which friends or relatives gather to share," Leo XIV said.At the end of the service, after official thanks from the bishop of Salto, Arturo Eduardo Fajardo Bustamante, the Pope presented a chalice to the local diocese.Leo XIV's programme in UruguayThe packed schedule for the day continued with an intense itinerary of institutional and pastoral engagements. After the liturgy in the park, a visit to the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary followed for the unveiling of a commemorative plaque and a greeting to the faithful outside the building. The Pontiff then left Paysandú for the capital, Montevideo, where the second part of his busy official agenda continued.In the late afternoon in the capital, the Pope will meet the social community of Casavalle at the Parish of Our Lady of Guadalupe. This will be followed by an engagement with the academic and education sector at the Catholic University of Uruguay. Both moments will be a central opportunity for direct dialogue with the educational and care institutions of the South American country.The day will conclude at Montevideo's Centenario Stadium, which the Pope will reach by travelling in the popemobile to allow once again for an encounter with the public. In the sports venue, Leo XIV will preside over a solemn prayer vigil together with thousands of young people and faithful who have travelled from all over the country for the closing event.On Sunday, the pope is expected in Florida, about 90 kilometres from the capital Montevideo, considered the "cradle" of the nation because it is where the Declaration of Independence took place in 1825. It is also an important religious centre due to the presence of the National Shrine of the Virgen de los Treinta y Tres. In the square in front of it the Pope will celebrate Sunday Mass.
